body.text: The internet really did change the world. Investors who bought internet stocks in March 2000 still lost most of their money. Being right about the future is not the same as being right about the price.

children.text: The dot-com bust is the most useful crash for a modern investor to study, because its central mistake is so easy to repeat. There was no fraud at the heart of it and no single leveraged blow-up. Millions of people correctly believed that a new technology would transform business, and then paid prices that assumed every company riding that wave would win. In India, the same mania lifted IT stocks to valuations of hundreds of times earnings, made Wipro's founder briefly one of the richest people on the planet, and set the stage for one of Dalal Street's biggest scandals.
The Displacement: The Internet Arrives

markDefs.definition: The late 1990s belief that technology had permanently changed how economies worked, making traditional business cycles and valuation rules obsolete.

children.text: By the late 1990s, the internet was moving from universities into homes and offices. E-commerce, online advertising and networking equipment looked like the industries of the future, and they were. Commentators spoke of a
new economy
in which old valuation rules no longer applied. The technology heavy Nasdaq Composite became the scoreboard of the mania.

stats.label: Nasdaq-100 Forward PE
stats.context: At the March 2000 peak, several times the long-run norm

stats.label: Cisco, 27 March 2000
stats.context: Briefly the most valuable company in the world

markDefs.definition: Dot-com era slang for the number of visitors or users a website attracted. It was used to value companies with little revenue and no profits.

children.text: As prices ran ahead of profits, investors changed the yardstick. When a company had no profits, analysts valued it on revenue. When revenue was tiny, they valued it on website visitors, often called
eyeballs
. Each step down the table below is a sign of euphoria.

body.caption: How the Yardstick Slipped During the Dot-Com Mania

cells: How much does the business earn?
How fast are sales growing, even without profit?
Optimism: profits assumed to arrive later
How many people visit the website?
Euphoria: revenue assumed to arrive later
Is it an internet company at all?
Peak mania: the story alone sets the price

body.title: Read the Yardstick
body.question: A research report values a loss making Indian startup IPO mainly on its "monthly active users" and compares it to a US company with ten times its revenue. According to the dot-com pattern, what does this valuation method signal?
options: A conservative valuation grounded in profits
A late stage signal, since the yardstick has moved away from both profits and revenue
Nothing, because user numbers are the same as cash flows
body.explanation: Users can be valuable, but valuing a company mainly on users means investors have moved two steps away from profits. In 1999 and 2000, the same drift from earnings to revenue to eyeballs was one of the clearest signals that prices had detached from business reality.

children.text: India's Own Tech Mania

Indian IT services companies had a genuine story: cheap, skilled engineers serving global clients, with Y2K fixes and the internet boom driving demand. In March 1999, Infosys became the first Indian company to list on a US stock exchange, on Nasdaq itself. The story was real, but by early 2000 the prices were not. Wipro hit its highest ever share price of ₹9,624 on 21 February 2000, and Forbes reported it had traded at hundreds of times its expected earnings. Azim Premji's roughly 75% stake was worth about $30 billion, making him the richest Indian in the world.

stats.label: Sensex High, February 2000
stats.context: Driven by IT, media and telecom stocks

stats.label: Premji's Wealth, by May 2000
stats.context: As Wipro's share price came back to earth

children.text: The smaller technology, media and telecom stocks rose, and fell, even harder. Zee Telefilms is a striking example. Its share price more than tripled in under five months, then collapsed by over 90%. Many of these stocks were favourites of a broker named Ketan Parekh, whose role in pumping them up is the subject of Chapter 4.

body.title: Your Turn: The Zee Round Trip
body.prompt: Zee Telefilms peaked at ₹1,555 on 24 February 2000 and fell to ₹121 by 30 March 2001. What was the peak to trough fall? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: Fall = (1,555 minus 121) divided by 1,555, times 100, which is about 92.2%. To get back to ₹1,555 from ₹121, the stock would need to rise about 1,185%. Even an investor who bought early, at ₹476 in October 1999, and held through the whole round trip lost about 75%.

children.text: The Pop: March 2000 to October 2002

There was no single trigger. The Federal Reserve had been raising interest rates since June 1999, which made future profits less valuable and borrowing costlier for cash hungry startups. Companies that had raised money on stories started running out of it. Once prices turned, the slide lasted two and a half years, broken by rallies that each proved temporary, just like 1930.

events.title: The Fed Starts Tightening
events.description: The US Federal Reserve begins raising interest rates from 4.75%, eventually reaching 6.5% by May 2000.

events.title: The Sock Puppet IPO
events.description: Pets.com, an online pet supplies retailer famous for its sock puppet mascot, lists at $11 a share.

events.title: India Peaks
events.description: The Sensex hits its high of 6,150.69 and Wipro reaches its record ₹9,624 on 21 February.

events.title: Cisco on Top of the World
events.description: Cisco Systems briefly becomes the world's most valuable company, worth over $550 billion.

events.title: Pets.com Shuts Down
events.description: Just 268 days after its IPO, Pets.com announces it will liquidate. Its shares trade at $0.19.

events.title: Shock on Shock
events.description: After the 11 September attacks, markets fall again. The Sensex hits its low of 2,594.87 on 21 September.

events.title: Trust Collapses
events.description: Enron and then WorldCom file for bankruptcy amid huge accounting frauds, and investors stop believing reported numbers.

events.title: Nasdaq Bottoms
events.description: The Nasdaq closes at 1,114.11, about 78% below its peak. It will not regain 5,048 until 2015.

children.text: Survivors and Casualties

The most important lesson of the bust is what happened to individual companies. Most internet and technology stocks crashed together. What happened next depended entirely on whether a real, cash generating business sat underneath the story.

body.title: After the Crash: Two Kinds of Companies

columns.label: Casualties
points: Pets.com: IPO in February 2000, liquidated in November 2000
Many businesses had customers but no path to profit, and burned through the cash they raised
Valuations were built on users and hype, with nothing left once the story faded
In India, many of the hottest small tech and media stocks of 2000 lost most of their value and never came back

columns.label: Survivors
points: Amazon: fell about 94% from its 1999 high, but kept growing sales and later became one of the world's largest companies
Infosys and Wipro: share prices fell hard, but revenue and profits kept growing through the bust
They had real customers, real revenue and a route to strong cash flows
Even so, investors who bought them at the 2000 peak waited many years to break even

body.caption: Amazon survived its crash, but a 94% fall needs a roughly sixteenfold rise just to get back to where it started.

body.label: Great Company, Terrible Price
body.value: Cisco: over 25 years to a new record
body.context: Cisco stayed a real, profitable business after 2000. Yet its share price did not close at a new record high until December 2025, more than 25 years after its March 2000 peak. The company was fine. The price paid for it in 2000 was not.

body.title: Quick Check
body.textWithBlank: Cisco's 25 year wait shows that a great company bought at a bad ___ can still be a bad investment.
body.explanation: Quality and valuation are separate questions. Asking "is this a good business?" is not enough. You also have to ask "what does today's price already assume?" In 2000, even the best technology companies were priced for perfection.

body.title: The Next Big Technology
body.scenario: A colleague is excited about a new technology theme. "This will change every industry, just like the internet did," she says. "I am putting my entire bonus into every listed Indian company that mentions it in its presentations. Some of them do not make money yet, but that does not matter when the market is this big." Several of the stocks she names have tripled in the past year.
body.prompt: Using the dot-com bust, explain what is right and what is dangerous about her reasoning. What would you want to know about each company?
body.modelAnswer: She may well be right that the technology is transformative. The internet did change every industry. But the dot-com bust shows three dangers in her approach. First, a correct view of the future does not protect you from overpaying: Cisco was a great business and still took over 25 years to regain its 2000 price. Second, buying every company that mentions a theme ignores that most companies in a new industry fail or get acquired cheaply, while a handful capture most of the value. Pets.com and many of India's hot tech stocks of 2000 had the right theme and no durable business. Third, putting an entire bonus into one theme concentrates risk, and stocks that have tripled already carry high expectations. For each company, you would want to know: how much revenue actually comes from the new technology rather than just presentations; whether the company is profitable or has a credible path to profit and enough cash to get there; how its valuation compares with its actual earnings or sales; whether promoters are selling shares into the excitement; and whether it would survive a 70% or 80% fall in its share price. The theme can be right while most of the stocks are wrong.

body.title: Is Every Technology Boom a Dot-Com Bubble?

children.text: Not necessarily. Every major technology wave, from railways to electricity to the internet, has drawn comparisons to earlier manias, and some booms are justified by genuinely strong earnings. A few questions help separate a boom from a bubble:
Are the leading companies profitable?
In 2000, many internet companies had no profits at all. A boom led by businesses with strong, growing profits is on firmer ground.
How far have valuations stretched?
Compare PE and price to sales ratios with the companies' own history and with growth rates, using the valuation stretch test from Lesson 1.2.
Where is the money coming from?
Heavy borrowing, a flood of IPOs from young loss making companies, and first-time investors piling in are all warning signs.
Has the yardstick slipped?
If analysts are moving from profits to revenue to users to justify prices, that is the dot-com pattern repeating.
No one can reliably call the top of any boom. The goal is not to predict a crash, but to know what you own and what its price already assumes.

body.title: Separate the Story From the Business on Screener.in
steps: Pick a technology stock you own or are considering and open its page on Screener.in
Check whether net profit has been positive for each of the last five years
Compare cash from operations with net profit, since reported profits should turn into real cash over time
Note the current PE ratio and compare it with the stock's own median PE over five and ten years
Compare the share price rise over the last three years with the growth in sales and profit over the same period
Check promoter holding changes over recent quarters for signs of promoters selling into the excitement
Write one sentence describing the business without using the theme's buzzword. If you cannot, treat that as a warning sign

body.label: Screener.in
body.description: Look up Wipro and Infosys and study their long-term price and PE charts. See how long a buyer at the February 2000 peak waited to break even, even though both businesses kept growing.

The belief that technology had made traditional business cycles and valuation rules obsolete.
Dot-com slang for website visitors, used to value companies with little revenue and no profits.
Market value divided by annual revenue. Used when a company has no profits, and a sign of stretched expectations when relied on heavily.
A US stock index heavy in technology companies. It fell about 78% from March 2000 to October 2002.
A group of Indian stocks favoured by broker Ketan Parekh during the 1999 to 2000 boom, many of which later collapsed.

points: The dot-com bubble rested on a real displacement, the internet, but prices assumed that every company riding the wave would win
Watch the yardstick: the slide from valuing profits, to revenue, to users, to a ".com" name was a clear euphoria signal
India had its own tech mania: Wipro hit ₹9,624 in February 2000, and the Sensex fell about 58% from its February 2000 high to its September 2001 low
Smaller hype stocks fell hardest: Zee Telefilms dropped about 92% from peak to trough
Survivors like Amazon, Infosys and Wipro had real businesses underneath, but even they crashed and took years to recover
A great company bought at an extreme price can still be a poor investment, as Cisco's 25 year wait for a new record showed
